Facebook's new suicide watch

By: Tarryn Crossman | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Facebook has launched a response to suicidal posts in South Africa

Summary:
We live in an age where teenagers express all their emotions on social media, they have no privacy boundaries. So it is not a shock that social media is more and more being used as a platform where people are crying out for help or posting their last suicide notes, this is the platform they are choosing to say good-bye

When Gugu found herself in the depths of a nervous breakdown she used social media as a way voice her darkest emotions. She explains how when she couldn’t confide in the people in her life she found social media safe space to say what she was feeling.

Noticing the amounts of suicide notes being posted on FB, FB has decided to do something in an attempt to solve the problem. They are working with SADAG and have launched a suicide or self-harm alert button locally. The button has been around internationally for a while now, but was launched in SA last month

Case study: Gugu - posted her suicidal thoughts on FB
Specialists: SADAG
Supporting material: animated FB, tumbler and Instagram posts of peoples suicides notes with their identities hidden.
Facebook has provided us with a video of they created for this new alert, we can use interviews from here
https://vimeo.com/160565004

Press Release:


Online Suicide Alert
We live in a world where more and more people—particularly teens—feel safe expressing their darkest emotions online. And, with 23 completed suicides taking place in South Africa every day, there is an increase in posts about self-harm and suicide. Facebook has recently joined forces with local depression group SADAG to provide an Alert button and support to desperate people. Carte Blanche asks: has social media become both cause and cure for cyber cries for help?


Script:


Time code CHARACTER / VISUAL
1 00:03 Bongani V/O

Facebook post and images of kids who have killed themselves Bongani: For Millennial social media has become a digital diary; it’s a place where they can express their every thought. Often revealing more than they would in person this has led to an increase in a number of posts of self-harm and suicide. In South Africa there are 23 completed suicides every single day a further 460 are attempted every 24hrs one in four have attempted suicide. Now if you put that in relation to a class of 30 learners it’s a terrifying number.
2 00:33 News clips of posts by teenagers who have killed themselves.

Music

3 00:40 – 00:57 Bongani interview with Liane Lurie – Psychologist Bongani: There is this belief that if someone is really serious about suicide then they are not going to talk about it. Is that a myth?

Liane: It is a myth; there is another myth that says that if somebody actually talking about suicide, are they then really going to do it?


4 00:57 SADAG Director Cassey Chambers Cassey: the main thing to remember there are many reasons that cause suicide but its so important you get help and you take it seriously. You know 75% of people who commit suicide tell someone first.
5 01:10 Emma Sadlie – Social Media Lawyer speaks to Bongani Emma: Now historically that would’ve been face to face vocally expressing that you have thought about committing suicide or maybe even that you have decided to, that you feel there is no other option and because of all of our communications in the real world have been taken online. That communication happens on a public platform.
6 01:26 Posts of on Facebook of teens reaching out and mentioning that they are going to kill themselves.

V/O V/O: Mitchell Parker is journalism graduate a thinker and a socialite. But he also suffers from bipolar which is a fact that everyone who follows him on social media would know, he has used social; media for years as a way to express his depression and anxiety and even had a way to say good bye when it got too much.
7 01:56 Mitchell Parker sits down in an interview with Bongani Mitchell: Because we have been living our lives more and more online, it is perhaps a better place to gage where someone is at. I know even the darkest moment of my life I found myself becoming a bit of a hermit becoming abit of a raucous but I was still very active on social media.

Bongani: What was your lowest moment where you posted a message on social media?
8 02:17 Mitchell and Bongani interview. Mitchell speaks of his lowest moment. Mitchell: I think the lowest for me was May 31st t about 21:00pm and yeah I was kind of sitting in my res room and something kind of unhinged its difficult even to this day to even describe the feeling that I had. It felt like everything was spinning and that if I didn’t something to kinda stop this spinning that the world would tilt off the side of its axis things would break. That’s why I ended up reaching into my medicine cabinet and taking a handful of pills. So I posted what was essentially just one word. I posted the word LOVE and then just a small x and strangely enough the one Facebook status that I would’ve wanted was “ Ahh Mich I love you too you are the best, but I got 1 like’

9 03:06 Mitch Facebook with one 1 like and link of Bongani Bongani: Due to a growing number of social media post about self harm and suicide Facebook has launched an alert button that seeks flag these when they are made but will it work and should other social; media platforms do the same?

10 03:22 Cassey Chamber of SADAG Cassey: So the new alert button is a suicide online reporting toll. So what happens if someone posts a comment you know” I’m not coping and I cain’t do this. Goodbye everyone” you as a friend or a loved one who is part of their friends group can actually report that status to Facebook. So its as way that someone a friend or family member can anonymously report their post and insure that they get some resources or intervention

Bongani: Is it available everywhere?

Cassey: it’s a GLOBAL insinuate that Facebook has launched and they have launched it already in Americas and Australia and the UK. And we are very excited that just two weeks ago they have launched it in South Africa and they have decided to partner with SADAG because we run the countries only suicide crisis helpline

11 04:06 Bongani speaks to Emma Bongani: So is the new alert by Facebook for suicide specifically going to work?

Emma: Well I don’t think it’s going to work but I think it’s a step top the right direction, and I think all these steps are to encouraged. We saw recently a case in India it happened just last month where a 21-year-old girl her face was photo shopped onto a naked body and these photographs where put onto Facebook. The girls father reported the photographs to Facebook, it took Facebook 5 days to delete that content during which time this 21 year old daughter committed suicide and so what the Indian authorities are doing in this particular province are looking at making Facebook a co-accused in the criminal charges that are to be brought against the person who had originally created the content and posted it.


12 04:55 Bongani speaks to Liane Bongani: can we put a positive spin on it and say,” actually social media allows this cry for help to be herd?”

Liane: Of course it does, very often people are ashamed to express those feeling when they are in trouble. But they are not coping in a world where coping is completely like emphasized and I think also people feel safer behind a computer screen as apposed to a one on one interaction
13 05:20 Mitchell speaking to Bongani with cut away of him walking away from coffee shop Mitchell: I think that it is important to be careful in the way in which you frame your social media self. So as to not put too much importance on it because I think that’s the dangerous road. But I do also think that in terms of power of social media and social networking and you know having these kind of communities is that you can us it as a platform to cry for help if need be.
14 05:44 Emma concludes about taking steps for helping others Emma: if I see one of my friends saying something I don’t know particularly emotional. Talking about suicide talking about how depressed they are that would be a big warning sign for me to go and take real steps, in the real world to make sure that that person feels like there is help available
15 05:41 Knocking on the premises. Captain Novela: We are the police if you don’t open for us we are going to break everything down.
Owner of the dog: Its up to you, you can break it. If I open for them they will fight me you know.
